name: Uridine (incl. triacetyluridine)
short: Uridine triacetate, used after fluorouracil or capecitabine overdose: vomiting, nausea, diarrhoea; may weaken those drugs. HIV trials: well tolerated; HDL fell in one, lipids unchanged in another.
text: Human safety data on uridine come from small trials and from the medicine uridine triacetate. In a 3-month randomised placebo-controlled trial in 20 people with HIV and antiretroviral-associated fat loss (lipoatrophy), a dietary uridine supplement was reported as well tolerated and did not affect the antiviral treatment, although HDL cholesterol fell in the uridine group while it rose with placebo. In a larger randomised trial in 165 people with HIV lipoatrophy, which used a supplement that the cited pharmacokinetic study found to be more than 90% triacetyluridine in its nucleoside content, only 59% completed 48 weeks of treatment, and three participants (one of them taking uridine) stopped because of diarrhoea; no changes were found in fasting lipids, and the authors described uridine as well tolerated, with no loss of control of the virus. An open-label case series of seven depressed adolescents with bipolar disorder reported uridine as well tolerated over 6 weeks, and a pharmacokinetic study in healthy volunteers (the abstract does not give their number) observed no adverse effects from a triacetyluridine-rich supplement or from pure uridine. Uridine triacetate was approved by the FDA as an emergency treatment after fluorouracil or capecitabine overdose or early severe toxicity, based on two single-arm trials in 135 patients; the most common adverse reactions were vomiting, nausea and diarrhoea. The same review states that uridine triacetate is not recommended for non-emergency treatment of side effects of fluorouracil or capecitabine because it may diminish the efficacy of these cancer drugs.
